questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Soil, Stains and Their Removal' refers to.
questions.a: Fabrics gather two kinds of soil: everyday dust and grease, and accidental stains -- tea, ink, curry, blood, rust. Each stain has a chemistry: fresh stains yield to prompt treatment; protein stains like blood need cold water; grease needs solvents; tannin stains like tea need acids. The rule is act fast and treat by type.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Soil, Stains and Their Removal'.
questions.a: Match the remedy to the stain -- cold for blood, solvent for grease, acid for tea -- and never let a stain set.

concepts.title: Laundering: Washing, Drying and Ironing by Fabric

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Laundering: Washing, Drying and Ironing by Fabric' refers to.
questions.a: Regular laundering follows a cycle -- sorting, soaking, washing, rinsing, drying, finishing -- tuned to the fabric: cottons bear vigorous washing and hot ironing; silks and woollens demand mild detergent, gentle handling and low heat. Sorting by colour and fabric protects the whole wash.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Laundering: Washing, Drying and Ironing by Fabric'.
questions.a: Sort, soak, wash, rinse, dry, press -- with the vigour scaled down for silk and wool, up for cotton.

concepts.title: Storage and Long-Term Care of Fabrics

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Storage and Long-Term Care of Fabrics' refers to.
questions.a: Between uses, fabrics need storage that blocks their enemies -- moisture, insects, dust and sunlight. Clean items only are stored; woollens get washed, sunned and packed with repellents; silks are wrapped; and periodic airing keeps long-stored textiles fresh and safe.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Storage and Long-Term Care of Fabrics'.
questions.a: Clean before you store, keep out damp, light and moths -- and visit the trunk between seasons.
